name: The Stoop Squeezed By The Driveway
aka: the landing that is a slab
symptom: A front door reached by one riser, or none, from a slab landing that is continuous with the driveway apron. Where there are steps, they are 5 or 6 in high and 14 in deep because the run was too short for proper ones, so the flight reads as a ramp with edges. The threshold is at the level a car door opens at, the door has no platform to be opened from, and the whole approach has no vertical event in it.

cause.explanation: The first-floor level is set by the garage. An attached garage's slab must meet the driveway at the property's grade, and the house floor sits one step above the garage slab - the code requires the change or a rated sill - so the entire building is anchored to the driveway's elevation. Every inch of first-floor height above that costs fill, stem wall, exterior steps and a steeper drive. Add an accessibility expectation for a level or near-level entrance and the floor drops to the ground, taking the base and the stoop with it.
cause.cost_saved: $4,000-$14,000 in fill, stem wall, exterior steps and drive regrading to lift the first floor 12 to 24 in.

rule_violated.statement: The house sits on a plinth and the water table stands 24 to 36 in above finished grade, which means the entrance is reached in three to five risers.
The front wall on the street line, entrance directly on the pavement with a stoop of 3-5 risers. Even the tightest urban condition in the kit keeps the risers.

rule_violated.ref: IRC R311.3 and R311.7 - landings at exterior doors, riser 7 3/4 in maximum, tread 10 in minimum, landing 36 in in the direction of travel
rule_violated.statement: The code requires a landing 36 in deep at every exterior door and caps the riser at 7 3/4 in. It says nothing about the minimum, so a 4 in riser and a 14 in tread is compliant, awkward to walk and reads as an accident - the code protects against falling and not against a bad stair.

rule_violated.ref: an entrance is marked by a rise
rule_violated.statement: Going up is the oldest threshold device there is, and it does three things at once: it raises the floor above the wet, it puts the visitor below the householder at the door, and it announces arrival. Three risers is the smallest number that does all three.

correct_practice: Set the first-floor level from the section, not from the driveway. Three to five risers to the front door is the traditional and the workable range, which follows from a first floor 18 to 30 in above finished grade with a water table at 24 to 36 in. Where there are steps, build them properly: risers equal within 3/8 in, 6 1/2 to 7 1/2 in high with 11 to 13 in treads, which is a gentler and more generous stair than the code minimum and is what every good stoop measures. Give the door a landing at least 5 ft by 5 ft rather than the 36 in the code asks for, because a landing is where somebody stands with an umbrella and a bag while the door opens outward past them. Where a level entrance is genuinely wanted - and it often should be - the correct answer is a graded approach on the long axis rather than a lowered building: a walk falling 1 in 20 over 40 ft gains 24 in of floor height without a ramp, a handrail or a visible accommodation, and it is the move that lets a house have both a base and a step-free entrance. Where a ramp is needed, integrate it as a terrace, a raised forecourt or a graded lawn walk rather than as a bolted-on incline.

fixes.right: Raise the first floor 24-30 in above finished grade, take the entrance in four risers off a 5 by 5 ft landing, and reach it by a graded walk rather than from the apron.
fixes.cheap: Fall the ground, not the house. Taking the grade down 8 to 10 in over the first 8 to 10 ft in front of the entrance, and building a low retaining edge at the walk, buys two extra risers and a base for $1,000-$2,500 with no change to the structure - and because the eye measures the base against the ground immediately adjacent, a very local fall does most of the work. Second move that costs nothing: separate the landing from the apron. Even a change of material and a 4 in step between the driveway apron and the entry landing turns a continuous slab into a threshold.
fixes.dishonest: Building up a wide flight of two shallow risers across the whole front of the house to make the entrance look grander. Wide shallow flights read as a plinth that is not there, they collect water at the door, and the riser height that results - usually 4 to 5 in - is exactly the dimension people trip on, because it is below the height at which a step is registered as a step.

detection: Count the risers at the front door in a photograph: three to five is correct, one or none is the fault. Then measure the riser height against the door: a 6 ft 8 in leaf divided into eleven gives 7 1/4 in, which is what a good riser looks like against a door in an image. Look at where the landing ends - if the paving runs continuously into the driveway apron with no change of level or material, the entrance is at car level. And check the threshold against the mulch: an entrance with fewer than two risers almost always also has a buried base and a water table at or below the ground.

test.note: 3 to 5 is the traditional range and follows from a first floor 18-30 in above grade. Countable in almost any front photograph. Where a step-free entrance is deliberate, the test is replaced by first_floor_height_above_finished_grade_in, which should still be at least 18, with the rise taken up in the approach walk instead of at the door.

exceptions.why: Hugging the ground is the type's whole formal argument and a one-riser or level entrance is authentic to it.
exceptions.bounds: The building must then also be low, horizontal and unstacked, and the entrance must still get a real landing and a sheltering overhang. A two-storey house with a ranch's entrance height is not an exception, it is the fault.

exceptions.why: 8-12 in above grade is the documented post-war figure for slab-on-grade work and gives one or two risers.
exceptions.bounds: Authentic where the whole building is minimal. Adding a portico or a full cornice reintroduces the series that the low entrance is missing from.

exceptions.why: The floor sits 12-36 in on low brick piers, which at the low end of the range gives two risers, and the galerie floor is the landing.
exceptions.bounds: The galerie must be there at 6-10 ft deep, or the abat-vent at 30-48 in. The porch is what makes a low entrance work in this type.

exceptions.why: The wall meets the ground directly and entrances are commonly at or near grade, often through a portal.
exceptions.bounds: Requires the portal or a recessed entry giving shelter and shadow; a flush door at grade in a flat wall is not this.

exceptions.why: The street door opens off the pavement with no rise at all; the threshold is made by the zaguan, which is a room-length transition rather than a vertical one.
exceptions.bounds: Requires the zaguan with a heavy street door and a cancela at the court end. A flush door with nothing behind it is not a substitute.

confused_with.difference: That is the same section failure read on the wall. This is it read at the door, and this one is the version the client actually feels, every day, arriving.
Unrelated despite the name - that is vents on the roof slope above the entrance.

That fault is the DIMENSION of the risers - an interior stair's proportions used outdoors. This one is the NUMBER of them, and a stoop can have correct 6 1/2 in risers and still have only one of them because the driveway set the floor level.

severity_by_style.why: The high stoop of 6-10 risers to a parlour floor 4-7 ft above the sidewalk is the type; a ground-level entrance converts it into a different building.
The plinth and its three to five risers are the base of the whole storey series.
A low or level entrance is the type's argument.
